claims.text: In tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloys, high-temperature plastic strain and toughness are primarily governed by coherent TiC nanoprecipitates.
Coherent TiC nanoprecipitates facilitate dislocation transmission across phase boundaries and reduce localized stress concentrations.
Reducing localized stress concentrations through coherent precipitates enables more uniform plastic deformation and enhances toughness at fusion-relevant temperatures.
Spark-plasma-sintered WxTaTiVCr-type alloys can initially contain minimal or incoherent TiC precipitates.
Adjusting sintering temperature and time can controllably produce coherent TiC nanoprecipitates in the proposed alloy.
Carefully designed thermo-mechanical processing can produce stepwise, controllable coherent nanoprecipitation in a tungsten refractory high-entropy alloy.
The relevant structural mediator is a uniform population of coherent TiC nanoprecipitates within a BCC refractory matrix.
Coherent precipitates relieve interfacial stress concentrations that could otherwise cause premature crack initiation.
Coherent precipitate interfaces facilitate dislocation transmission.
The engineered coherent-precipitate alloy will have greater high-temperature plastic strain capacity than a baseline containing few or incoherent precipitates.
The engineered alloy will exhibit greater high-temperature toughness and energy absorption than the baseline.
The engineered alloy will maintain high strength at approximately 800 °C.
The coherent TiC nanoprecipitates will remain stable and coherent during high-temperature exposure.
The proposed effect requires precipitate volume fraction, size, and spacing to remain within an optimal range that avoids coarsening and deleterious intermetallic phases.
Temperatures around 800 °C and above represent fusion-relevant operating conditions for the proposed comparison.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement in plastic strain capacity, toughness, or energy absorption would falsify the proposed hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention changes sintering temperature and time, while the comparison is described as having identical processing history except for nanoprecipitate control. Because precipitate state is generated by the changed processing history, the proposed groups cannot literally have identical processing histories, and processing-related confounding is not fully isolated.
